description: We are GU Boys, a dedicated 3-member team of avid computer science students who love taking on tough engineering challenges. With a clear split between 1 coder, 1 designer, and 1 idea maker, we focus on transforming complex data into highly interactive, polished web applications. We accept the challenge to build something visually stunning and highly functional for this year's hackathon.
summary:
MARSWALK is a mission-control map for planning a human Marswalk in Jezero Crater. We fused real NASA and USGS data (CTX imagery, a 20 m elevation model and slope, USGS geology, CRISM spectral data, THEMIS thermal inertia, and MEDA/MARCI weather context) into one layered interface on a Mars-specific grid. On top of it, an A* routing engine computes walking routes using real Mars geometry, with a choice between shortest distance and gentler terrain. In our test, the terrain-priority route reduced the steepest segment slope from 13.3° to 8.7° for 13% more distance. A mission-profile planner (science, settlement, safety-first) and a first-person walking interface connect site selection to the walk itself.

This addresses the challenge by turning scattered orbital data into a hyperlocal, multi-layer tool for one excursion. It matters because astronauts will have limited oxygen, bulky suits and delayed contact with Earth, so they need clear, honest guidance. Every layer shows its source and limits, and we make no safety claims beyond what the data supports.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

MARSWALK is a mission-control map for planning a human Marswalk in Jezero Crater. It works in four steps:

  1. Acquire real data. Scripts download NASA and USGS datasets and verify their checksums. Raw files are never overwritten.
  2. Build one grid. A 20 m elevation model is cropped to 5 x 5 km (250 x 250 cells), with an expanded 7.5 x 7.5 km view. It uses a Mars-specific projection (sphere radius 3,396,190 m). Slope is computed from each cell's neighbours using real Mars distances. Imagery, geology, CRISM spectral data and THEMIS thermal inertia are aligned on the same grid.
  3. Plan routes. An A* pathfinder searches the grid and the user chooses between shortest distance and gentler terrain. In our test, the terrain route cut the steepest segment from 13.3° to 8.7° for 13% more distance (3,507 m vs 3,964 m).
  4. Present it. A web interface shows the layers, route comparison, source values and limits. A prototype planner recommends sites by mission profile (science, settlement, safety-first), then a first/third-person walking view with a HUD and minimap lets the user experience the route.

What are the benefits?

  • Replaces scattered data silos with one layered view for a single excursion.
  • Gives astronauts a trade-off (shorter or gentler) instead of a single opaque answer.
  • Every layer shows its source, units, resolution and limits, so users know what to trust.
  • Results are verifiable: A* costs match Dijkstra, and 94 automated tests (60 Python, 9 JavaScript, 25 browser) back the pipeline.

What is the intended impact?

To move Mars data from regional, scientist-facing tools toward hyperlocal, astronaut-facing planning. The same pipeline can be reused for other Mars sites and, later, for the Moon. It is also meant to set a standard for honest safety tooling: a map that says what it cannot show.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?

Area

Tools

three.js

Data sources

NASA/JPL Mars Trek, USGS Astrogeology, PDS (CTX, DEM, THEMIS, CRISM, MEDA, MARCI, RAD)

Testing

Python tests, JavaScript tests, Chrome browser tests

Version control

Git and GitHub

Hardware

Standard laptops and a desktop web browser (no special hardware)

If your team used AI coding assistants, state that here. Space Apps asks teams to disclose it.

How is it creative?

  • Honesty as a feature. Each layer carries its limits, and the interface avoids safety or mineral claims the data cannot support.
  • Two routes, one choice. Side-by-side comparison puts the astronaut in control of the trade-off.
  • From planning to walking. One flow links site selection, landing and a first-person walk, instead of showing only a static map.
  • Mars-native math. Distances and slopes use Mars geodesic geometry, not Earth map formulas.
  • Auditability. Provenance, hashes and independent verification scripts make results reproducible.

What factors did we consider?

  • Astronaut safety first: we show slope and terrain context but make no travel-safety certification.
  • Data limits: 20 m cells miss small holes and rocks, geology has 100-200 m registration offsets, CRISM is valid on only part of the grid, and Jezero has no measured radiation dose (Gale's RAD is labelled separately).
  • Cognitive load: a simple HUD and minimap, with layers off by default.
  • Communication delay: 3 to 22 minutes one-way, so tools must work locally.
  • Suit mobility and metabolic cost: modelled through explicit round-trip assumptions, with suit-specific limits planned.
  • Reproducibility and scope: a small, well-verified site rather than a large, unverified one.
